implementation_notes: Kotlin's lazy collection is Sequence: the stdlib documents that multistep processing runs lazily when the result of the whole chain is requested and classifies operations as intermediate (lazy) or terminal (forcing), with generateSequence(seed, next) and sequence {} building bounded or unbounded sources. A sequence is iterated on demand and is not memoized, so repeated traversal recomputes (asSequence() over an iterator is single-use, while one built by a function re-iterates); Kotlin's own documentation warns that the lazy overhead can outweigh the benefit for small collections, where List and its eager operators remain the simpler choice.
pitfalls: A Sequence obtained from asSequence() on an Iterator is single-use, while one from a collection/factory re-iterates - the interface hides the difference, so an API returning Sequence may throw or recompute on a second traversal.
Sequences are not memoized: a terminal operation run twice repeats all element work, and a sequence holding a large closure/coroutine context retains it.
For small data or simple operations the per-element lambda and indirection cost makes sequences slower than a List loop, which the documentation explicitly warns about.

variants.name: kotlinx.coroutines Flow (asynchronous lazy stream)
variants.idiom_name: flow { emit(x) } / flowOf with map/filter/take collected by collect{}
variants.implementation_notes: Flow is Kotlin's asynchronous lazy sequence: a cold, coroutine-based stream whose builders (flow {}, flowOf, asFlow) suspend inside emission and whose operators (map, filter, take, flowOn) stay lazy until a terminal collect runs in a coroutine, so element production suspends rather than blocks and cancellation propagates structurally. It is the right realization when each element requires awaited work or when the consumer itself is in a coroutine; the synchronous Sequence remains simpler and cheaper when nothing suspends, and SharedFlow/StateFlow are the hot, multi-consumer counterparts rather than lazy collections.
pitfalls: A Flow is cold and single-subscription by design: collecting twice restarts the whole source, and a flow built from a hot/shared channel needs shareIn/stateIn instead.
Cancellation is cooperative: a blocking call inside flow {} ignores cancellation, so use withContext(Dispatchers.IO) and cancellable suspending APIs.
Exceptions inside a flow propagate to the collector and cancel the scope; bare try/catch around emit can break exception transparency (prefer catch/retry operators).
